title: Facial recognition in public places

turns.speaker: Hugo
turns.text: The cameras at the station are running live facial recognition now. There's a sign, in fairness, but it's about this big.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: And matching against what? That's the thing nobody says.

turns.speaker: Hugo
turns.text: A watchlist. Which is compiled by them and isn't published.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: The accuracy figures are the part I'd push on. They quote ninety-nine per cent, but that's on a small list under good lighting.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Ninety-nine sounds fine until you multiply it by fifty thousand people a day.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Exactly. One per cent of fifty thousand is five hundred false matches before lunch.

turns.speaker: Hugo
turns.text: Which in practice means being stopped, and in practice that falls on the same faces every time. The error rates aren't even across skin tone and everyone testing it has found that.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: The argument for it is the ten people it does catch, though. That's not nothing either.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: No, and I don't want to pretend it is. The question is whether we'd accept the same trade if it were done by hand.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Stopping five hundred people a day to find ten would be a scandal. Automating it doesn't change the arithmetic, it just hides it.

turns.speaker: Hugo
turns.text: That's the clearest way I've heard it put.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: I'd still want it at a stadium on a match day. Different situation, consented entry, known risk.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Agreed, actually. It's the walking through a station without choosing anything that I object to.

points: Live facial recognition is running at a station, signposted only minimally, matching against an unpublished watchlist.
Nadia notes the quoted 99 per cent accuracy comes from small lists in good lighting.
At fifty thousand passengers a day, one per cent error means around five hundred false matches, which in practice means being stopped.
Hugo adds that error rates are uneven across skin tone, so the burden falls repeatedly on the same people.
Nadia's central argument is that stopping five hundred people to find ten would be a scandal if done manually, and automation hides the arithmetic rather than changing it.
They agree the case differs where entry is consented and the risk is known, such as a stadium, as against walking through a station.
